Abstract

This paper documents the system that produced FPLAgent's current 2026/27 Gameweek 1 recommendation. The objective is not to make the most confident-looking forecast. It is to make the strongest decision that the available evidence supports, preserve its lineage, and expose the conditions under which that decision should change.

The published squad is R-01afc86b1b, a £100.0m 3-4-3 captained by Bruno Fernandes. It emerged from a fresh 537,804-squad local and global search, was rescored in independent 25,000-world five-week and eight-week holdouts, survived a high-scoring stress, exact autosub and scoring-rule ablations, and remained the lowest-regret compromise across the five-week model-risk family and the eight-week transfer/horizon family. The five-week specialist R-b954c5c198 has lower five-week regret, but the published squad wins the eight-week audit and the declared cross-family synthesis. It also ranks first in the independent structure stress. Those agreements and disagreements are retained as evidence rather than hidden: the synthesis chooses the squad with the best declared balance, not the squad favoured by the last test that happened to run.

The system's strongest demonstrated edges are: leakage-safe player forecasting that beat the declared form baseline in 11 of 12 time-forward shortlist slices; a legal GW1 picker that recorded two wins, one tie and no losses across three historical seasons; opponent-adjusted match rates that beat a simple Poisson benchmark on both frozen seasons; a bounded Betfair defender feature that improved time-forward defender selection in all three tested seasons; exact FPL rules and correlated simulation; wide local and distant squad search; and explicit robustness, horizon, bench and availability vetoes.

The paper also draws a hard line around evidence that has not earned production authority. Understat is collected and replayed but currently receives zero weight. Clear two-source RotoWire/FFScout lineup consensus has bounded provisional role authority, while disagreement stays conservative and visible. Price timing, full distribution calibration and chip timing are implemented as measurement frameworks, not promoted decision signals. No 2026/27 event has yet finished, so no honest claim can be made that the engine is objectively best in the world. The defensible claim is narrower and useful: this is the best-supported current GW1 decision produced by the declared, checksum-bound FPLAgent process.

1. The decision, in plain English

1.1 What the engine is solving

Before Gameweek 1 the manager must choose 15 players, a legal starting XI, a captain, a vice-captain and an ordered bench under a £100.0m budget and the live club/position rules. That is already a joint decision. A cheap substitute can be false economy if a starter misses out; a player with the best opening fixture can be a poor purchase if he immediately creates a transfer problem; and the highest mean XI can be fragile if its result depends on one optimistic minutes assumption.

FPLAgent therefore asks:

Given only information available before the current deadline, which legal 15-player squad and GW1 configuration offer the best robust points route through the opening schedule, while preserving the ability to adapt as new information arrives?

The default utility is FPL points. Ownership, novelty, team value and visual symmetry are not rewards in themselves. Ownership can be evidence about market expectations and later becomes relevant to mini-league risk, but the preseason engine does not buy a player because he is popular or reject him because he is template.

1.2 What “best” means here

“Best” does not mean highest displayed GW1 xP. The selected squad's direct GW1 lineup forecast is 64.29 points in the final synthesis artifact, while the exact one-week structure stress scores it at 60.23 under that audit's independent component world. Those values answer different questions and use different scoring paths. The connected current squad is 0.13 points higher on raw GW1 xP, but loses the validated multiweek decision; treating that tiny one-week edge as decisive would discard transfer value, later fixtures and model-risk evidence.

The production selector minimizes regret. For each declared scenario it measures how far a squad falls behind that scenario's leader. It then penalizes both average regret and worst-case regret. This deliberately accepts that the true model is unknown. A candidate that is second or third everywhere can be a better FPL decision than a candidate that is first in one favourite model and poor everywhere else.

1.3 Claim boundary

The system can defend the following statement:

R-01afc86b1b is the best-supported GW1 squad produced by FPLAgent under the current immutable evidence, legal rules and declared risk policy.

It cannot yet defend these stronger statements:

  • that the realized GW1 score will be high;
  • that no ungenerated legal squad is better;
  • that FPLAgent is already proven state of the art against every strong public or private model;
  • that its p10 and p90 simulation tails are empirically calibrated for 2026/27;
  • that a role, injury or transfer reported after the snapshot is already reflected; or
  • that a strong process will be spared ordinary football variance.

This distinction matters. A decision system is credible when it states where its evidence ends.

2.1 Why Bruno Fernandes is captain

Captaincy is solved inside the legal XI, not in a disconnected chat heuristic. The simulator doubles the captain's realized score and moves the multiplier to the vice-captain only when the captain plays zero minutes. Bruno remains captain across the published five-week, horizon and GW1 configuration receipts. An independent 25,000-world XI/configuration holdout promoted Mbeumo as vice-captain and Milenković ahead of Truffert on the bench.

This is a model decision rather than a certainty claim. The app must quote the same versioned captain receipt everywhere; a language model is allowed to explain the answer but not invent a different captain from stale context.

2.2 What is genuinely uncertain

The final availability watch found zero official-attention players, complete club-feed coverage, and two role-verification items among the 15: Watkins and McAteer. Preseason lineup absence is not treated as an injury label. Instead, the engine runs conditional appearance stresses and requires attributable deadline evidence before changing the production probability.

The role audit found that alternative squads can win under deliberately adverse Watkins-like appearance assumptions. That is a verification trigger, not a silent automatic transfer. The correct operational action is to check authoritative team news, translate confirmed evidence into the appearance model, and rerun the whole pipeline. Manually swapping one player would break the joint optimization of budget, XI, bench and later transfers.

The pipeline observed the published official generation at 15:28:23 UTC and released it only after all 15 stages completed. The canonical machine artifacts are the synthesis result, robust audit, horizon audit, structure stress, role scenario, role threshold and pipeline manifest listed in Appendix C.

3. Architecture: many vetoes, one decision

The design separates questions that fail differently:

  1. What was knowable before each deadline?
  2. How strong are the teams and fixtures after opponent and venue adjustment?
  3. What is each player's probability of appearing, minutes class and point return?
  4. How should bookmaker, component and independent-source evidence be weighted?
  5. How do correlated match events become exact FPL scores?
  6. Which legal squads merit expensive simulation?
  7. Which result survives alternative scoring, horizon and role assumptions?
  8. Is the whole artifact set coherent enough to publish atomically?

The executable flow is:

An LLM is not in this chain. The fine-tuned Qwen adapter powers conversation and explanation, but it does not set xP, choose a squad or resolve contradictions. Numeric tools produce a receipt; the chat layer is grounded on that receipt. This separation prevents fluent prose from becoming an unreviewable decision rule.

4. Data, temporal correctness and source authority

4.1 Official current state

The official FPL application endpoints remain authoritative for the live game definition:

  • bootstrap-static for player identifiers, clubs, positions, prices, statuses, events, chips and rule fields;
  • fixtures for the schedule, venue, kickoff and event allocation;
  • event-live and authenticated manager data for finalized outcomes and the manager's actual squad, bank, transfer state, purchase/selling prices and chips when those become available.

The current immutable snapshot contains 587 players, 20 teams, 380 fixtures and 38 events. The forecast pool contains 568 modeled players over eight events, or 4,544 player-event rows. Official FPL ep_this, ep_next and equivalent expected-points values are prohibited from the production feature allowlist. FPLAgent is therefore not repackaging the game's own forecast.

4.2 Historical corpus

The core historical player table contains 244,425 player-gameweek training rows. Vaastav's public FPL archive supplies player and match history, while stable FPL player code is preferred to the season-specific element ID for identity joins. Historical fixtures and teams support the opponent model. Smaller public manager datasets support behavioral audits such as initial-squad retention, transfer banking and bench context; they are not labels that tell the model to copy a winner.

The catalog exposes 14,351,814 rows through 158 views. Size is not evidence of quality. The edge comes from temporal contracts, stable mapping, explicit nulls and validation.

4.3 Point-in-time reconstruction

Final historical files can contain facts learned after the deadline: later injury statuses, rescheduled fixtures and final prices. The feature pipeline selects the latest archived state observable before an inferred deadline. Rolling windows end at the previous event. Same-gameweek minutes and points are labels only. Missing pre-era xG is null, not a fabricated zero.

The current data gate has 22 declared checks and zero failures. It tests duplicate keys, player identity, lag correctness, deadline order, forbidden feature presence, fixture coverage, adjusted ratings, live-rule consistency and current forecast completeness. A passing gate does not prove the data are perfect; it blocks known leakage and schema failures before they can influence a decision.

4.4 Authority ladder

More sources are not automatically better. A source adds edge only when its mapped, timestamp-safe signal improves legal FPL decisions. Otherwise it adds correlated noise, fragility or false confidence.

5. Feature engineering and regression to the mean

5.1 Player-deadline feature set

The production player model uses 47 features. They include lagged points and minutes, 3/5/10/38 event form, start and appearance rates, goals, assists, xG, xA, BPS, clean sheets, defensive contributions, price, ownership percentile, availability, set-piece order, cold-start state, opponent-adjusted team attack/defence, venue, expected goals for/against, clean-sheet probability, promoted-club priors, sample size and rest/staleness.

Official fixture difficulty and the old raw rolling team-goal features are excluded from the champion. They remain available only as controlled challengers. Feature availability is a contract: if a signal could not have been observed before the deadline, it cannot enter the row.

5.2 Why the engine does not chase last week's points

Recent points combine underlying opportunity with finishing, saves, bonus ties and other noise. A lagged historical audit compared three-event form with ten-event form after controls. Only 9.1% of the short-versus-medium-term deviation persisted into the next event, which is strong evidence of mean reversion.

The process split makes the idea concrete. Hot midfielders/forwards with strong underlying xGI/90 continued at 4.13 points next event, while hot players with weak process fell to 3.05. Cold players with strong process recovered to 3.69, compared with 2.87 for weak-process cold players. The lesson is not “ignore form.” It is “separate repeatable role and chance generation from noisy recent conversion.”

A 10% process-reversion correction improved the untouched 2025/26 continuous replay by 23 net points, while naive form chasing made 91 transfers, paid 212 hit points and finished 301 net points behind the selected reversion policy. The correction still remains shadow-only because its four-event uncertainty interval crossed zero. The production advantage today is therefore discipline: the main forecast already pools longer history and underlying process, while an unproven extra correction is not promoted simply because its total looked attractive.

5.3 Cold starts and epistemic uncertainty

New signings, promoted players and players with thin Premier League histories have wider model risk. Search diversification records:

Uncertainty combines disagreement between seeded models, a cold-start surcharge and a thin-history penalty. This is one search view, not a replacement for the central mean. It helps generate squads that do not all inherit the same optimistic newcomer assumptions.

6. Opponent-adjusted team and fixture model

6.1 Online hierarchical ratings

Each club carries shared attack and defence ratings plus smaller home/away residuals. Before a fixture the expected scoring rates are:

The expected rates are recorded before the result updates the state. All matches in the same kickoff batch are predicted before any of them update ratings, preventing a simultaneous fixture from leaking into another. Ratings decay, venue effects are partially pooled, and promoted teams start from a cohort prior rather than an invented Premier League record.

6.2 Demonstrated edge

The selected online team model uses a 540-day shared-rating half-life, 240-day venue half-life, 0.03 base learning rate and 0.01 venue learning rate. It was evaluated on 1,140 frozen fixtures: goal MAE 0.933, Poisson deviance 1.089 and clean-sheet Brier score 0.170.

A separate CUDA Poisson goal model was trained on 5,643 team-fixture rows and beat the simple home/away Poisson baseline on both untouched seasons:

Test seasonSimple Poisson devianceFPLAgent goal-model devianceResult
2024/251.1881.109FPLAgent lower
2025/261.1261.084FPLAgent lower

This is a direct competitive advantage for defenders, goalkeepers and attackers because it improves the shared estimates of team goals and clean-sheet probability rather than relying on the official fixture-difficulty badge.

7. Player appearance and points forecast

7.1 Position-specific hurdle model

The champion artifact is named forecast_v3_opponent_adjusted. Goalkeepers, defenders, midfielders and forwards have separate bundles. Each bundle contains:

  1. a four-class minutes classifier for DNP, 1–59, 60–89 and 90+ minutes; and
  2. a points regressor trained only on appearances.

For player features x:

Two XGBoost models with seeds 17 and 43 are averaged for each target and position. The training receipt records 244,425 rows, XGBoost 3.3.0 and CUDA execution on an RTX 5090. The GPU allows more time-forward experiments; it is not itself an accuracy claim.

7.2 Time-forward forecast evidence

The model is trained only on seasons preceding each test season for 2023/24, 2024/25 and 2025/26, giving 12 position-season slices. Against an availability-adjusted five-game form baseline it records:

  • 11/12 MAE wins;
  • 6/12 within-event rank wins;
  • 11/12 top-shortlist wins;
  • 7/12 GW1 top-shortlist wins;
  • +0.512 actual points per selected player-gameweek on the general shortlist; and
  • +0.418 actual points per selected player-gameweek on the GW1 shortlist.

The legal GW1 replay is more important than row-level accuracy. On identical historical budgets, club rules, XI, captain and bench selection, the FPLAgent picker beat the form baseline twice, tied once and lost zero times across the three tested seasons, for +18 realized points in total. Three seasons are not enough for a universal claim, but this is the right shape of evidence: forecasts must improve legal actions, not merely spreadsheet metrics.

7.3 Appearance recalibration

A logistic recalibrator is tested only on the top xP and xP-per-price population that the optimizer is likely to select. It must improve both Brier score and log loss in both forward tests. Only forwards passed every comparison, so only forward probabilities are recalibrated. Goalkeeper, defender and midfielder calibrators were rejected.

That rejection is a feature of the process. An intuitively plausible calibration cannot alter the squad unless it generalizes through the predeclared gate.

8. Independent football evidence

8.1 Understat

Understat supplies an independent view of prior-season shot quality and chance creation. It is not treated as an xP oracle: FPLAgent retains ownership of minutes, fixtures and scoring. Only data from the prior completed season are joined to a target season.

The time-forward results were mixed. Some midfielder/forward slices improved MAE or top-k return; others deteriorated. The exact legal decision replay selected a 0% blend in all three seasons. Understat is therefore valuable research coverage but currently contributes no production weight. This avoids the common mistake of assuming that a respected football metric must add incremental FPL value after the incumbent already contains related xG/xA signals.

8.2 Predicted lineups

RotoWire is the primary predicted-XI feed and FFScout is the independent cross-check. Captures are immutable and deadline-bound. The consensus scorer will compare predicted starters with actual starters, by club and event, and then replay the signal through the legal squad/XI/captain policy.

At publication, zero events have completed. The signal has zero production authority. It must reach at least six completed events, achieve two-source coverage on at least ten teams per event, show positive mean hit-rate lift, avoid a negative event floor and clear an uncertainty bound before it can even enter a challenger replay. This is particularly important for current role questions: source disagreement should widen uncertainty, not masquerade as a precise minutes cut.

8.3 Why SofaScore and FBref are not dependencies

The SofaScore challenger produced a small player-row MAE improvement but lost 15 points in the matched legal FPL replay. Its public endpoint also returned live HTTP 403 responses. It receives zero weight and normal deadline refreshes do not depend on recollecting it. FBref automated access also returned HTTP 403, and third-party wrappers inspected locally ultimately call the same web pages or invoke browser CAPTCHA handling. The system keeps Understat and the predicted-lineup pair, with soccerdata reserved for future research, rather than building a fragile bot-evasion dependency.

9. Betting markets as a bounded team prior

9.1 What is collected

The current market generation uses delayed public Betfair Exchange Match Odds and over/under 2.5 markets. Competition and market identifiers are discovered rather than hardcoded. Prices are de-vigged, timestamped and mapped to official fixtures. The current GW1 snapshot covers 10 of 10 fixtures; GW2–GW8 have no market coverage yet and therefore fall back to the internal team model.

The forecast records the exact market receipt and Parquet hashes. A transient provider failure may retain a checksum-valid, exact-fixture ready generation for no more than six hours; the failed observation is stored separately. A stale, wrong-event or incoherent generation still fails closed.

Markets inform team scoring and clean-sheet context. They do not directly declare that a specific player will start, take penalties or receive bonus.

9.2 Why the active weights are only 20% for defenders and 5% for forwards

An unconstrained one-season search selected a 70% market weight and then lost 16 points on the independent season. That failure is precisely why weight selection needs sequential stability. The bounded 20% defender blend improved top-k realized points and MAE in all three forward seasons:

SeasonDefender top-k liftDefender MAE improvement
2023/24+0.084 points/player-GW+0.0082
2024/25+0.128+0.0098
2025/26+0.160+0.0048

At 20%, frozen initial-squad decisions gained 27 realized points. The continuous development paths gained 64 and 76 points, and the frozen 2025/26 follow-up gained 90 points, or 2.368 per gameweek. The four-event moving-block interval was +0.816 to +4.132 per gameweek. However, the pooled out-of-selection lower bound crossed below zero. Production authority is therefore deliberately split:

  • preseason defender squad/XI decisions: 20% market blend;
  • preseason FWD goal-environment adjustment: 5% after a separate position-specific calibration;
  • preseason MID goal-environment adjustment: 0%, because its promotion test did not pass;
  • weekly transfer decisions: 0% until stronger continuous or prospective evidence passes.

This is one of the clearest competitive edges in the system because it combines a near-efficient football market with strict protection against overfitting that market.

10. Current-rule components and correlated simulation

10.1 Why marginal xP is insufficient

Independent xP addition misses football dependencies. One goal can create attacker points while removing clean sheets from several opponents. A starter DNP activates an ordered substitute only if the resulting formation remains legal. Captaincy depends on realized appearance, not just mean points. A coherent decision therefore needs shared match worlds.

10.2 Component models

Separate event models predict goals, assists, bonus and saves from point-in-time features. Goals, assists and bonus passed their time-forward gates. Saves failed the rank requirement and remain on an empirical fallback. The direct points model anchors residual player value so explicit match components do not discard signal that the component family cannot yet explain.

The 2026/27 scoring layer includes appearance, goals, assists, clean sheets, goals conceded, defensive contributions, saves, bonus, discipline and penalties. Historical BPS reconstruction exactly recovered all 2,415 bonus points across 380 control fixtures. The defensive-contribution proxy improved player-season MAE from 15.20 to 11.36 and Spearman rank from 0.786 to 0.892 on its frozen historical test; the promoted current-rule layer applies to outfield positions.

10.3 Monte Carlo world construction

For each fixture, the simulator samples correlated team scores from calibrated goal rates, assigns goals and assists to eligible players, samples minutes/appearance jointly, reconstructs FPL point components and bonus, and aggregates all fixtures in an event. The same random world is reused across candidate squads within a stage. That paired design removes much of the simulation noise from squad differences.

Identity checks enforce goal allocation, assist-to-goal limits, six bonus points per match, appearance marginals, fixture counts, and empty/double-fixture handling. The current eight-week holdout simulated two million match scenarios with 5,544,813 team goals; only 31 were unattributed, for a 1.0 reconciliation rate at the reported precision.

10.4 Exact FPL configuration scoring

Every deep candidate is scored as a full 15:

  • a legal XI with one goalkeeper, at least three defenders, at least two midfielders and at least one forward;
  • goalkeeper-only goalkeeper substitution;
  • ordered outfield autosubs subject to the post-substitution formation;
  • captain-to-vice fallback only on zero captain minutes; and
  • the current per-component scoring table.

The initial optimizer's small bench coefficient is only a candidate-generation proxy. It has no vote in the final structure gate, which exhaustively challenges all synthesis finalists and five bench-proxy settings with actual DNP worlds and legal autosubs.

11. Legal optimization and search breadth

11.1 Hard constraints

Every generated squad must satisfy the live budget, exact position counts, maximum players per club, 15-player roster, 11-player formation, captain/vice eligibility and ordered bench rules. Future policies also carry free transfers and prohibit the five-week/horizon planner from silently spending hit points.

The initial linear objective is a search instrument:

The final selector never treats this proxy as truth. It uses exact shared-world scoring and regret. The separate weekly action engine adds the historically calibrated terminal value of a banked free transfer when a planning horizon ends; that value is not smuggled into this initial squad proxy.

11.2 Global and local candidate generation

The 19 August run began with 144 seed squads covering residual/component models, horizon decays, formations, bench bands, premium structures and transfer-aware views. It generated:

  • 281,267 legal exhaustive same-position one-swap squads;
  • 518,272 local one/two-swap squads;
  • 256 distant mixed-integer squads at least three swaps from every seed; and
  • 19,249 evolutionary squads across legal crossover and mutation.

After deduplication the universe contained 537,804 legal candidates. Within the 10,000 retained discovery field, all legal formations and four bench bands were represented. Search breadth is an edge because a sophisticated evaluator cannot rescue a squad it never generates.

The five-week leader R-b954c5c198 records weighted mean regret 0.503, worst regret 1.244 and robust regret 0.688. 13. Eight-week horizon and transfer policy

13.1 Why an eight-week audit exists

Optimizing only GW1 can buy eleven good fixtures and four future problems. Treating all eight weeks equally creates the opposite error: it pretends today's injury and role information is still precise two months later. The engine evaluates a portfolio of horizons rather than declaring one natural constant.

The central 0.88 decay gives GW1 weight 1.00 and GW8 weight 0.88^7 = 0.409. Alternative views use 0.70, 0.80 and 0.94, plus separate GW1–3, GW1–5 and equal-weight GW6–8 scenarios. Fixed, open and forced-GW2-roll paths distinguish squad quality from optimistic transfer execution.

13.2 Outcome-based calibration

A separate rolling historical replay re-optimized at every deadline using only out-of-fold forecasts, carried legal squad and transfer state, and realized autosubs/captaincy. Selection on 2023/24–2024/25 preferred five weeks at 0.88, but it tied the eight-week incumbent on the untouched 2025/26 GW1–8 path. The candidate failed local-support and positive-test gates, so production kept the broader eight-week/0.88 sensitivity portfolio.

This result prevents a convenient story. The engine uses eight weeks as an adversarial adequacy audit, not because history proved eight to be universally optimal.

13.3 Current disagreement

The horizon audit promotes R-01afc86b1b, the eventual published 3-4-3. It beats the provisional five-week incumbent R-b954c5c198 by 1.654 decayed central points, with a paired interval of +1.524 to +1.784. Its horizon robust regret is 0.552, versus 1.848 for the five-week leader.

The disagreement is therefore clean and measurable: R-b954c5c198 owns the strongest five-week model-risk score, while R-01afc86b1b owns the horizon, structure and final synthesis. FPLAgent retains both facts rather than presenting every audit as unanimous.

Public manager histories support early optionality and later adaptation, not a fixed eight-week team. In the 2025/26 top-100 trail, 61 managers rolled in GW2, only 22 in GW3 and 19 in GW4. Those observations shape stress design but are descriptive and survivorship-selected; they do not set the decay coefficient.

14. Cross-family synthesis

For every candidate measured in both families:

The 20% maximum-family term penalizes specialists that are excellent only because one model family likes them. Both inputs remain in FPL point-regret units; they are not rescaled to manufacture a preferred answer.

The five-week specialist wins when horizon-family weight is below 15.5%; the published 3-4-3 is champion from 15.5% through 100%. The declared 50/50 policy lies well inside the published champion interval rather than on a convenient boundary.

15. Bench allocation: rotation, not bench worship

The £20.0m visible bench initially looks expensive. The targeted audit asked whether the model was overvaluing reserves.

Sixty-eight targeted candidates received fresh five- and eight-week simulations, including all 39 protected squads at or below £18.5m and 120 shortlisted squads at or below £20.0m. The active squad was the exact targeted winner. This is a matched opportunity-cost test, not a historical claim that an expensive bench is intrinsically valuable.

The mechanism is rotation. Three of the four GW1 substitutes are scheduled to start later and the group supplies eight planned starts across GW2–5. Truffert is planned for GW2–5, Milenković for GW3–5 and Verbruggen for GW4. McAteer is the one current non-rotator. The system is purchasing a flexible 15, not expecting £20.0m to remain unused.

Recent elite examples show observed opening/early-wildcard benches from £18.5m to £21.0m, but that evidence is descriptive. The production rule is not “spend more on the bench.” It is “score all 15, test cheaper matched alternatives, and keep depth only when autosub and planned-start value beats the opportunity cost.”

16. Structure, scoring and role stress

16.1 Scoring and formation stress

Every synthesis finalist and five bench-proxy challengers was rescored under central rules, bonus removed, defensive-contribution points removed, both removed, and both doubled. Exact autosubs and captain fallback were used in all views.

The stress-specific leader was the published R-01afc86b1b. It scored 60.226 in the central component view and ranked first across the five-view regret selector, with robust structure regret 0.125. The next candidate scored 60.075 centrally and 0.285 robust regret. Structure therefore supports rather than merely tolerates the cross-family decision on this snapshot.

16.2 Preseason role scenarios

The role audit perturbs conditional appearance rates for players repeatedly absent from independent preseason lineups and for players with low recent start shares. Baseline, moderate, severe and not-listed-DNP boundary scenarios are tested in independent residual and component worlds. Winning challenger squads are given the same exhaustive 550-configuration XI, bench, captain and vice search as the incumbent.

Alternative squads lead some deliberately adverse role worlds, so the resulting verdict is material_counterfactual_reversal_requires_live_verification, while production_changed remains false. A second causal audit then checks whether each apparent reversal is actually created by a drop from the player's live minutes anchor. On this snapshot every individual challenger already won its narrow GW1 comparison at the production anchor, so none was mislabelled as a minutes threshold. The combined severe-role alternative gained 0.589 in its GW1 family but carried 4.125 more multiweek synthesis regret; it remains monitor-only rather than an executable fallback. Conditional stresses are not source-authoritative probabilities. Their purpose is to identify which news requires a full rerun. At publication, Watkins and McAteer are the two selected players requiring role verification.

16.3 Availability gate

The pipeline cannot publish a partially refreshed decision. Official status/news, price, fixture, forecast, market, participation and role lineages are checked together. A stale or incoherent availability watch blocks publication and retains the last valid workspace. On the current run all clubs had feed coverage, no player had official-attention evidence, and the Watkins/McAteer role items were surfaced as scenario attention.

17. External benchmark and competitive evidence

Internal baselines are necessary but insufficient. A strong system should face a method it did not invent. FPLAgent reproduces the public OpenFPL modeling shape—position models and matching feature contract—on identical point-in-time folds and passes both models through the same legal £100m squad, XI, bench and captain solver.

The matched benchmark contains 84,999 player-deadline forecasts, 12 position-season folds and 114 legal event decisions:

ModelMAERMSELegal policy total relative to FPLAgent
FPLAgent0.97791.94090
OpenFPL-method reproduction0.99341.9373-69 points

OpenFPL won the 2023/24 legal path by 41 points; FPLAgent won 2024/25 by 103 and 2025/26 by 7. The benchmark therefore passes, but it is one reproducible public method—not proof that every external model has been beaten. It provides meaningful competitive evidence because the comparison uses the same rows and legal decisions rather than different leaderboards or post-hoc examples.

18. Season-long decision engine

The preseason squad is the first state of a longer system. Once the season begins, the dominant question shifts from “which 15 should I buy?” to “given my actual squad and state, should I roll, transfer, take a hit, change XI/captain or use a chip?”

18.1 Weekly state and transfers

The authenticated manager state includes the actual 15, XI, captain/vice, bank, free transfers, purchase prices, selling prices and chips. Weekly action generation supports roll, one-transfer, multi-free-transfer and paid-transfer routes, always rebuilding the best XI and captain from all 15. FPL's half-profit selling rule is modeled exactly. A terminal value for banked free transfers was learned from historical replay so the horizon does not spend a transfer merely because the last visible week has no value for saving it.

The initial-squad five/eight-week audits deliberately allow no hits. Paid transfers matter after the manager state exists and are evaluated net of four-point costs in the weekly engine.

18.2 Blanks and double gameweeks

The schedule receipt classifies confirmed, provisional and unassigned fixtures. Component outcomes are simulated per fixture and then aggregated to the FPL event, so a player can have zero, one or multiple matches. Historical double-gameweek rotation informs appearance handling. Unresolved rearrangement probability remains shadow-only and blocks authoritative chip timing rather than being guessed.

18.3 Chips and expiry

The 2026/27 rules provide Wildcard, Free Hit, Bench Boost and Triple Captain once in each half of the season—eight chip slots—with first-half expiry after GW19. The engine represents permanent Wildcard squad replacement, temporary Free Hit restoration, exact Bench Boost scoring and captain tripling, transfer-bank transitions and one-chip-per-event legality.

Chip searches and historical retention replays exist, but their downside gates have not passed. Operational advice therefore remains no_chip unless and until retained option value is validated. This fail-closed behavior is a competitive advantage over a horizon that spends a chip simply because it cannot see a better opportunity beyond its endpoint.

18.4 Price and execution timing

Current/purchase/selling prices and future affordability stresses are modeled. A prospective rise/flat/fall collector and net-points timing scorer exist, but preseason has produced zero price nights and zero timing decisions. Price forecasts receive no authority. Team value is diagnostic; only realized net FPL points can promote an early-transfer policy. Until then the operational recommendation is to wait for information unless the exact decision receipt has stronger evidence.

20. Why we are confident—and why variance still matters

Confidence comes from convergence of independent protections:

  1. The forecast is independent of FPL's own expected-points field and beats a declared simple baseline on time-forward and legal-decision tests.
  2. Team scoring rates beat a simpler fixture model on two untouched seasons.
  3. The only external live forecast feature with production weight—Betfair at 20% for defenders and a separately calibrated 5% goal-environment blend for forwards—passed bounded gates; midfield and more aggressive weights remain at zero.
  4. The selected structure emerged from more than half a million legal candidates and survived distant optimization, not just swaps around a favourite team.
  5. Final comparisons use shared correlated worlds, exact autosubs and independent holdouts.
  6. Five-week model/scoring risk and eight-week horizon/transfer risk disagree, and the final squad is the best balanced answer across both rather than a hidden cherry-pick.
  7. Bench spend, scoring rules, formations and role uncertainty received dedicated adversarial tests after synthesis.
  8. Publication is atomic and checksum-bound; stale partial runs cannot silently replace the last coherent decision.
  9. A matched public-model reproduction gives external evidence rather than relying only on internal baselines.
  10. Unproven complexity is kept at zero authority, reducing the risk of an impressive but fragile preseason model.

None of those protections eliminates football variance. A 64-point expectation is an average over many possible worlds, not a promise. Red cards, penalties, deflections, late injuries and bonus ties can dominate one gameweek. Even a genuinely superior season-long policy can lose a mini-league over 38 events. The goal is to repeatedly choose actions with positive expected value, control avoidable downside and update when evidence changes. The “variance gods” still get a vote.

21. Prospective 2026/27 proof plan

The current readiness verdict is DEADLINE_GRADE_RESEARCH_SYSTEM_NOT_SOTA_PROVEN: all ten production gates passed in the readiness audit, while only one of six research-frontier gates had passed before the season.

Every deadline will freeze the forecast, available alternatives and chosen action before outcomes. After finalization the scoreboard will measure:

  • player MAE, rank and legal decision points;
  • appearance Brier score and log loss;
  • OpenFPL-method and other matched challengers;
  • RotoWire/FFScout lineup hit-rate and legal-policy lift;
  • CRPS, 50%/80% interval coverage, p10/p90 tails by position;
  • captain, starter and bench tail calibration;
  • price-direction Brier/log loss and net-points timing value; and
  • regret of squad, transfer, XI, captain, bench and chip decisions using only pre-deadline options.

Six completed events trigger diagnosis, not promotion by anecdote. At least 19 are required before the first formal SOTA evidence claim, and even that must pass matched benchmark and decision gates. The system is designed to learn from this season without rewriting history after seeing outcomes.

22. Reproducibility and operations

22.1 Transactional refresh

The web app refreshes official evidence on open only when the prior coherent decision is too old or a semantic input changed. The current schedule is six hours outside T-24, two hours from T-24 to T-3, and 30 minutes inside T-3. Manual refresh bypasses reuse. Price, availability, fixture, market-generation or forecast checksum changes trigger the full pipeline immediately.

A full run stages outputs separately and publishes only when all gates pass. Closing the browser does not cancel the backend process. If a run fails, the previous published workspace remains active and the UI exposes the blocking receipt.

22.2 Hardware-aware acceleration

The production workstation pairs an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 (Blackwell, 31.4 GiB visible VRAM) with a 16-core/32-thread Ryzen 9 9950X3D. The validated software path is NVIDIA driver 610.43.02, CUDA 13.2 runtime / 13.3 driver API, CuPy 14.1.1 and XGBoost 3.3.0. FPLAgent treats the CPU and GPU as two different compute engines, not as a reason to send every operation to CUDA. The accelerator router chooses the measured faster deterministic implementation for each workload:

WorkloadProduction deviceWhy
XGBoost player, component and team-goal inferenceRTX 5090 through CUDA/CuPyModels are CUDA-trained; device-native arrays avoid XGBoost's CPU DMatrix fallback and repeated host/device copies.
XGBoost training and time-forward model experimentsRTX 5090Thousands of boosted-tree fits and challenger folds are the clearest Blackwell throughput advantage.
Independent squad and transfer-policy MILPs12 isolated CPU processesHiGHS is CPU-native. One thread per worker avoids scheduler contention while independent policies fill physical cores.
Four independent preseason role scenariosFour isolated, single-threaded CPU processes over memory-mapped worldsSeparate interpreters bypass the Python GIL; read-only simulation tensors are shared rather than serialized four times.
Current exact autosub and sparse screening kernelsCPUProduction-shape benchmarks found transfer and pattern construction dominated; forcing these kernels onto CUDA was marginally slower.
Future sufficiently large dense simulation kernelsRTX 5090 when the measured operation gate is crossedCUDA remains available behind an explicit size threshold rather than being used cosmetically.

This routing has three consequences. First, CUDA inference stays on the RTX 5090 end to end: CuPy supplies device-resident float32 matrices to XGBoost and the refresh test records zero device-mismatch warnings. Second, independent optimization is genuinely parallel. The exact 20-sample initial-squad stability audit fell from 152.999 seconds to 23.519 seconds on the same inputs, a 6.505× speed-up, with byte-equivalent decision statistics. Four representative open/rolled transfer-policy pairs improved from 15.083 to 6.913 seconds (2.182×), and eight GW1–8 challenger solves improved from 7.757 to 3.684 seconds (2.105×). The full 128-squad residual discovery population is now generated in about 18 seconds; two immediate runs produced the same population hash and every squad passed the legal validator. The previously dominant preseason role-scenario audit fell from 639.824 to 197.632 seconds (3.237×) after moving its four independent counterfactual worlds from GIL-limited threads to isolated processes backed by memory-mapped input tensors. Its complete result remained exactly equal to the published serial reference. The rejected thread experiment managed only 618.999 seconds, which illustrates why acceleration changes are benchmarked rather than accepted from architecture diagrams alone. The final production publication independently recorded 198.629 wall seconds, 671.167 CPU seconds and 3.38 average CPU cores for this stage, confirming that the benchmark translated to the transactional pipeline rather than only to an isolated script.

Third, the router records when the GPU is not an advantage. On the production exact-autosub shape of 25,000 worlds × 512 candidates × five events, CPU scored in 25.786 seconds and CUDA in 26.151 seconds, with identical scores. A sparse 100,000-world utility screen was also dominated by CPU because it completed before PCIe setup could be amortized. Automatic mode therefore keeps these shapes on CPU and only moves a kernel to CUDA above the benchmarked operation threshold. “Fully using the hardware” means minimizing wall time, not making the GPU utilization graph look busy.

The competitive edge is indirect but important: more independent challengers, deeper untouched holdouts and more role/fixture stress can finish before the deadline. Blackwell does not make a forecast more accurate by itself; it buys the experiment budget needed to reject weak ideas and validate useful ones. Seeds are generated in the parent process, worker results are restored to a stable order, and equality/legal checks guard every accelerated boundary. The pipeline manifest records wall time, aggregate CPU time, average cores and peak memory per stage so future routing changes must earn their place empirically.

Operators can reproduce or override the router with FPLAGENT_ACCELERATOR=auto|cpu|cuda, FPLAGENT_POLICY_WORKERS=<n>, FPLAGENT_ROLE_WORKERS=<n> and FPLAGENT_GPU_MIN_MULTIPLIES=<n>. auto is the production default; forced CUDA exists for controlled benchmarking and fails loudly if the device is unavailable.

22.3 Rebuild command

Individual research commands are documented in the linked audit reports. The canonical deadline run should use the transactional pipeline rather than manually composing a partial sequence.

22.4 Seed discipline

Simulation seeds are versioned by purpose. Discovery, selection, five-week holdout, high-goal stress, horizon selection and horizon holdout use independent streams. Changing a seed is a sensitivity test; repeatedly changing it until a preferred squad appears is not valid research.

23. Limitations and failure modes

23.1 Shared model risk

The direct xP model helps generate candidates and anchor component means. Independent holdouts remove Monte Carlo selection noise, but they do not eliminate a shared wrong belief about a player or team. The external data and market program is intended to reduce this risk only when incremental legal-policy evidence is positive.

23.2 Search is broad, not exhaustive

There are vastly more legal budget/club-valid combinations than 537,804. MILP restarts and evolutionary search give global reach, but the engine cannot prove an ungenerated squad would not win. Protected benchmarks, one/two-swap enumeration and distant finalists make the search claim stronger without turning it into a mathematical global proof.

23.3 Tail metrics are model-world diagnostics

Current p10, p90 and CVaR values compare candidates under shared simulated worlds. They are useful for relative downside selection. They are not yet proven calibrated prediction intervals, because zero 2026/27 events have been scored by the prospective distribution framework.

23.4 Current-role uncertainty

Predicted-lineup feeds have bounded authority only for clear two-source starts; source disagreement retains the incumbent role probability, and every selected premium, starter and armband must still clear a separate capital/lineup integrity gate. Post-World-Cup preseason participation remains unusually difficult to interpret. The Watkins verification item is real. The answer should be rerun after credible press-conference or squad evidence rather than assuming the current receipt is permanent.

23.5 Season-long frontiers

Ordinary weekly transfer mechanics are operational, but price forecasting, schedule-rearrangement probability and retained chip value remain unpromoted. The system can calculate candidate actions; it intentionally refuses to authorize the speculative parts until their point-in-time replays pass.

23.6 Source and rights risk

Public accessibility is not a commercial redistribution licence. This project is a local research system. Any public product would need source-specific rights review, retention rules and paid data contracts. Endpoints can change; every source needs a checksum, freshness policy and zero-authority fallback.

24. Final deadline protocol

Before entering the team:

  1. Refresh after the final relevant press conferences and near the GW1 deadline.
  2. Verify Watkins and any new official status, transfer or registration changes.
  3. Confirm all ten GW1 market fixtures still map cleanly; missing markets must fall back to the internal team model rather than stale prices outside the six-hour validated retention window.
  4. Rebuild the forecast and complete all 15 pipeline stages when the semantic fingerprint changes.
  5. Require the data, structure, role, availability and transactional publication gates to pass.
  6. Compare the new receipt with R-01afc86b1b: squad, XI, captain, bench, family regrets and role items—not only the headline GW1 xP.
  7. Treat a minutes fallback as executable only when the central squad wins at the live anchor, a monotone deterioration creates the reversal below it, and its GW1 floor repays multiweek regret.
  8. Freeze and hash the final receipt, then enter that exact legal team in FPL.

If no material evidence changes, reusing the checksum-identical receipt is more rigorous than rerunning repeatedly and interpreting Monte Carlo noise as new information.

25. Conclusion

FPLAgent's competitive case is not one clever formula. It is the accumulation of disciplined small edges and vetoes. Point-in-time reconstruction blocks leakage. The player model improves on recent form. Opponent-adjusted rates improve fixture context. A carefully bounded market signal adds defender information. Correlated simulation values all 15 players and exact game mechanics. Global search challenges roster assumptions. Independent holdouts reduce selection noise. Regret and horizon families stop one model from owning the answer. Bench, structure, role and availability audits attack the final squad from different directions. Atomic publication stops incoherent artifacts reaching the app.

The current result is a 3-4-3 built around Bruno Fernandes captaincy, a rotating £20.0m nominal bench and two selected role-verification items. It is supported more deeply than the earlier squad, but it is still a decision under uncertainty. The strongest reason for confidence is not that every model agrees—they do not. It is that disagreement is measured, the selected squad remains near the frontier across those disagreements, and unsupported signals are prevented from voting.

That is the standard the project should carry through the season: freeze what was known, choose the best legal action, expose the counterfactuals, score the result honestly, and improve only when the new method earns its place.
